lead: Today’s readings share one sad note: what might have been. Through Isaiah God sighs over a people who would not listen: “O that you had paid attention to my commandments!” Psalm 1 sets the two ways side by side. In the Gospel Jesus compares his generation to sulking children who will not join any game. God is not hard to please; it is we who find reasons not to answer.

set: Chapter 48 closes the first part of the Book of Consolation (Isaiah 40–48), which has been speaking of Cyrus and the fall of Babylon. Just after our passage comes the call “Go out from Babylon” (48:20). Before sending the people home, God looks back on why they were in exile.
str: v. 17: God’s self-introduction: Redeemer, Holy One, teacher, guide.
v. 18: the wish: if only you had listened.
v. 19: what they would have had: descendants like the sand, a name that lasts.
kw: Well-being in every part of life. The NRSV has “prosperity”, the POC has “peace”. Both are part of the word’s meaning.
The NRSV has “success”, the POC has “justice”. The word means being in right order with God and neighbour, and the good that comes from it.
vv: I am the Lord your God, who teaches you for your own good, who leads you in the way you should go.
God’s commandments are not a test to catch us out. They are the teaching of someone who wants our good.
O that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your prosperity would have been like a river, and your success like the waves of the sea;
This is the voice of disappointed love. The river never stops and the waves keep coming: that was the life God wanted to give.
your offspring would have been like the sand, and your descendants like its grains;
This recalls the promise to Abraham (Genesis 22:17). God’s promise has not been withdrawn: the very next verses send the people home.
ch: The Catechism calls the moral law the work of divine Wisdom, “fatherly instruction, God’s pedagogy”, which shows the ways that lead to the promised beatitude (CCC 1950). Isaiah’s God who “teaches you for your own good” is the same. In Advent these words are a call to examine our conscience before Christmas: not to despair over what might have been, but to listen today.

set: Jesus is still speaking about John the Baptist (11:7–19). He compares “this generation” to children in a marketplace, playing at weddings and funerals. Some children call out, and the others will not play either game. So people reject John as too severe and reject Jesus as too friendly.
str: vv. 16–17: the parable of the children.
vv. 18–19a: its application: John and the Son of Man are both refused.
kw: Those of that time who refused to respond. Jesus’ words are not about a whole people: many in Israel followed him, and the warning is for every generation, ours too.
God’s saving plan. In Matthew 11 Jesus speaks and acts as God’s Wisdom.
vv: ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we wailed, and you did not mourn.’
Flute for a wedding, wailing for a funeral. John’s call to repentance is the dirge; Jesus’ meals with sinners are the wedding.
For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon’;
the Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is vindicated by her deeds.”

A note on the text. Some manuscripts read “by her children”, as in Luke 7:35. The reading “deeds” is the better attested in Matthew, and it recalls “the deeds of the Messiah” in 11:2. The insult “friend of tax collectors and sinners” is, without meaning to be, a true description of him.
ch: The Catechism notes that Jesus scandalised the Pharisees by eating with tax collectors and sinners as familiarly as with themselves (CCC 588). That table continues in the Eucharist. The passage warns us not to make God fit our own taste: he comes in the way he chooses, in the austere voice of John and in the warm welcome of Jesus.

qa: Is Jesus blaming the Jewish people here?

No. “This generation” means those who refused to answer him, and many of his own people did answer: all his first disciples were Jews. The Church firmly rejects any such blame (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598). The words are addressed to us, who also find excuses.
study: What excuse do I use most often when God’s call comes in a form I do not like?
“O that you had paid attention”: what is one thing God has been asking me for a long time, which I could begin today?
